idea: Compare bus/contract performance only after normalising for factors outside the operator's control (peak speed, vehicle utilisation, spread of hours): regress gross cost per in-service km on those factors, then replace each operator's context values with the sample median to get net cost/km and benchmark against the median.
does: Compares bus lines or scenario variants on cost per bus-km and passengers per bus-km after removing congestion speed and utilisation effects
inputs: per-line or per-run bus-km, bus-hours, peak vehicles, mean peak speed, passengers
outputs: gross vs net cost/km, passengers per bus-km, benchmark pass/fail
notes: Use to judge whether a TSP gain is real vs. congestion differences; needs bus passenger loads (not built).

idea: Subsidy/cost per passenger = cost per bus-km divided by passengers per bus-km (CE / NE); minimum standard X passengers per bus-km; shadow fare when below X. Gross cost per bus-km calibrated as linear function of avg peak speed, km per bus, evening/weekend share, peak vehicle requirement (Table 8.1; speed coefficient -0.0228 $/km per km/h).
does: Reports cost per bus-km, passengers per bus-km, cost per passenger for each bus line in a run and effect of speed change from TSP/bus lanes on cost
inputs: bus run stats from results: bus-km, service hours, speed, peak fleet, boardings
outputs: CE, NE, $ per passenger, speed sensitivity
notes: Gives TSP experiments an economic output (operating cost saved by speed gain).

idea: Bus service quality index (SQI): apply stated-preference utility weights (generic MNL; reliability/on-time, fare, access time, travel time, safety, ride smoothness/jerky braking, headway, driver) to each passenger's experienced attribute levels; operator SQI = mean utility, normalised to lowest operator = 0. Travel time, access time, fare dominate. Smooth ride (no jerky braking) is a positive attribute.
does: Scores each simulated bus line by a utility index built from simulated headway, punctuality (minutes late), in-vehicle time, walk/access distance to stop and a ride-smoothness count (harsh decelerations)
inputs: run results per bus line: schedule adherence, headway, travel time, stop spacing, hard-brake counts
notes: Weights must be assumed (not calibrated); label as placeholder. Harsh-braking count is computable from vehicle accel in sim. Ch9 finds higher SQI correlates with LOWER cost/km (coef -0.36 on ln SQI).

idea: Random-effects regression of 46 BRT systems: fare elasticity -0.366, headway elasticity -0.243/-0.294 (frequency elasticity ~+0.30), plus dummies (pre-board fare collection +0.63 ln pts, integrated network +0.41, modal integration at stations +0.45, doors both sides +2.1, independent quality oversight +0.76, station spacing/density -0.17).
does: Predicts the change in bus ridership/mode share when a scenario changes bus headway, travel time, fare or stop spacing, using the elasticities as defaults
inputs: baseline bus flow, headway change %, fare change %
outputs: scenario bus demand, plus label of assumptions
notes: Headway elasticity -0.29 matches meta-analysis (Hensher 2008, 241 obs: fare -0.395). Gives experiments a demand feedback so TSP/bus-lane improvements shift mode share.

idea: Report variance inflation factor VIF_k = 1/(1-R_k^2) for each regressor and flag values over 10; random-effects regression to handle grouped observations.
does: Adds VIF column to the regress tool output and warns on collinear regressors
notes: Stdlib-only: needs R^2 of each regressor on the others; small normal-equation solver.

topic: Gross/net performance ratio for bus lines
idea: Gross performance ratio GPR = (boardings per service-km) / average headway, where average headway = (peak + inter-peak + weekend)/3; net performance ratio normalises for priority-lane share, route type, direct competition via regression.
does: Ranks bus lines in a run or scenarios by boardings per bus-km relative to headway, with priority-lane share as a normalising variable
inputs: bus line stats and % of route in bus-priority lane/TSP
notes: Table 18.2 also gives a taxonomy of priority treatments (dedicated carriageway, dedicated lane, signal priority/queue jumps, premium stations) useful to label scenarios.

idea: Crowding valued as in-vehicle time multiplier: seated 1.0 (load factor 80%) to 1.83 (200%), standing 1.5 to 2.37; by standees/m2 seated 1.0->1.63, standing 1.53->2.04 at 6/m2. Sydney: crowded seat 1.17, stand<=10 min 1.34, stand >20 min 1.81, crush 2.04. Generalised cost 8.45 AUD/h + crowding 1.47-6.88 AUD/h.
does: Converts bus passenger-hours into crowding-weighted passenger-hours using load factor or standees per m2
inputs: bus load (people) vs seats and standing area per vehicle type, in-vehicle time
cite: Ch 22 s22.2, Table 22.3; Whelan & Crockett 2009; Wardman & Whelan 2011
notes: ACMS knows vehicle occupancy but passenger loading at stops is not built; would apply to assumed occupancy.

idea: Dwell time functions: boarding 2.3 s/passenger uncrowded rising to 2.9 and 4.4 s with 10 and 15 through-standees per door (cubic term, Puong 2000); Chicago bus: dwell increases with (standees)^2 x boarders+alighters (Milkovits 2008); Sydney: +0.34 s boarding and +0.56 s alighting per passenger when aisle has standees (Tirachini 2013).
does: Replaces the fixed 20 s dwell with dwell = fixed door time + per-passenger boarding/alighting times that rise with standees
inputs: boardings, alightings, onboard standees, payment technology
notes: Needs passengers at stops (not built); a stochastic version (Poisson arrivals per stop) is a first step. Dwell variability drives bunching and the TSP value.

idea: Full bus leaves passengers, next bus dwells longer and closes headway behind it, amplifying along the route (Abkowitz & Tozzi 1987); headway variance raises average waiting time (Welding 1957: E[W] = (H/2)(1+CV^2)); countered by holding control.
does: Measures headway coefficient of variation per stop and expected waiting time = (mean headway/2)(1+CV^2); shows if TSP worsens bunching
inputs: bus arrival times at stops across a run
outputs: headway CV, excess wait time, bunching count
notes: Cheap and directly relevant to TSP evaluation; buses exist in sim with headway. Suggests a holding-at-stop control as a TSP/agent action.

idea: Mohring square-root rule: optimal frequency grows with sqrt of demand (precisely demand^0.5-0.8 when boarding/alighting and bus-stop congestion counted); with crowding disutility optimal frequency and capacity are higher; bus queueing at stops depends on frequency, passengers transferred and fare technology.
does: Suggests a bus headway for a corridor given demand, value of waiting time and operating cost per bus-hour
inputs: passenger demand/h, bus cost per hour, value of time, cycle time
notes: The book states the rule qualitatively, no closed form with constants; implementer must state assumptions.

idea: Segregated bus lanes beat mixed traffic under fare/toll constraints (Mohring 1983; Basso & Silva 2010: one bus lane raises welfare vs any shared scenario; needs fewer buses, lower fare, higher frequency), ignoring turn-ban costs at intersections.
does: Preset experiment comparing bus lane vs mixed traffic on a corridor reporting person-weighted delay of bus vs car
notes: Person-weighted (bus occupancy) delay is the metric; ACMS counts people carried.

idea: Meta-analysis of 319 public transport direct elasticities: fares mean -0.395 (SD 0.274, n=241), in-vehicle time -0.547 (SD 0.374, n=57), headway -0.287 (SD 0.184, n=21); commuters less sensitive to fare and in-vehicle time but more to headway; RP estimates larger than SP.
does: Supplies default elasticities with +-1 SD ranges so scenario tests of bus fare/headway/travel time changes can run low/central/high demand responses
inputs: change in fare, in-vehicle time or headway; trip purpose (commuter or not)
notes: Pair with bus_demand_response; the SD band is the honest uncertainty for experiments.

idea: Crowding benchmark standards: unacceptable above 4 standees/m2 (Europe, Australia), 5 (USA, ITDP BRT peak), 8 (China); load factor not above 1.2 (USA); PiXC = (passengers - capacity)/passengers for the critical point, benchmark 4.5% peak.
does: Flags simulated bus segments exceeding a standees/m2 or load-factor standard and reports passengers in excess of capacity
inputs: bus load by link, standing area, seats

idea: Compare modes by full-fuel-cycle g CO2e per passenger-km; strongly depends on occupancy (urban bus 120-130 g/pkm, car ~200, electric rail 100-130); energy per pkm = vehicle energy / (load x distance), bus 0.92 MJ/pkm at 33% occupancy.
does: Reports fuel/CO2 per passenger-km and per vehicle-km for each vehicle type in a run, so bus priority or mode shift scenarios show an environmental result
inputs: vehicle-km by type, speed profile, occupancy
outputs: g CO2e per pkm by type, scenario difference
notes: No emissions/fuel KPI exists in the tool list; need a per-type fuel rate vs speed/acceleration (assumed); the book gives only aggregate intensities.

topic: Cost-benefit analysis of a corridor change
idea: Traditional BCR from travel time, vehicle operating cost, safety and emissions at a stated real discount rate (7% NSW, 4% elsewhere, 3.5% UK); BCR changes materially with the rate; wider economic benefits add a mark-up (16-23%) without changing ranking in the case.
does: Turns the difference between two simulated scenarios (person-hours saved, vehicle-km, crashes, emissions) into annual benefits, NPV and BCR at a chosen discount rate and horizon, with the rate shown as a sensitivity
inputs: two runs, value of time, capex, opex, discount rate, years
notes: Gives run_experiment an economic conclusion. Value of time, annualisation factor and capex are assumptions to state.

idea: Simulated shared-fleet replacement of cars: removing all private cars cuts vehicles but raises vehicle-km by 6.4%/day; with 50% private cars kept up to +90.9% km; with 40% of private cars kept, peak vehicle-km fall 13%.
does: Scenario preset testing mode substitution into shared taxis/minibuses, measuring VKT and congestion
inputs: share of car trips moved, fleet occupancy
notes: Needs dispatching of shared vehicles; large effort, low fit.
